questions.question: Q: What were the obligations of a good host under xenia?
questions.correctAnswer: To provide food, drink, bathing, comfortable rest and a gift before asking the guest's name or business. The host must not harm the guest, who is under Zeus's protection.

questions.question: Q: How does Polyphemus violate xenia?
questions.correctAnswer: He refuses to give Odysseus food or shelter, asks no questions about his identity, traps him in the cave and eats his crew — the complete inversion of proper hospitality.

questions.question: Q: Why are the suitors' actions a violation of xenia?
questions.correctAnswer: They consume Odysseus's food and wine, abuse his servants, court his wife and refuse to leave — they are guests who exploit their host's absence rather than respecting his home.

questions.question: Q: How does Eumaeus demonstrate proper xenia?
questions.correctAnswer: Despite his poverty as a swineherd, Eumaeus gives the disguised Odysseus food, shelter, warm clothing and respect — true hospitality is about generosity of spirit, not wealth.

questions.question: Q: Why was xenia so important in the ancient Greek world?
questions.correctAnswer: Without hotels or formal diplomacy, xenia enabled safe travel, trade and communication between cities. It was protected by Zeus and violating it risked divine punishment.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response How far does the Odyssey show that xenia was the most important social value in the Greek world? (15 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: The Odyssey presents xenia as the most important social value in the Greek world, though it also shows that other values like loyalty, courage and family were essential. Xenia structures almost every episode of the poem: Odysseus's reception by the Phaeacians, Circe, Aeolus and Eumaeus shows good xenia, while Polyphemus and the Laestrygonians show its violation. The suitors' abuse of xenia is the central conflict of the second half of the poem — their crime is primarily against hospitality, not against Odysseus personally. The fact that their punishment is death shows that violating xenia was a capital offence in the moral world of the Odyssey. Furthermore, xenia is divinely protected by Zeus Xenios, giving it a religious authority that no other social custom enjoys. The contrast between Eumaeus's generous xenia (despite his poverty) and the suitors' exploitation (despite their wealth) shows that hospitality reveals true character. However, other values are also crucial in the Odyssey. Loyalty (Penelope's faithfulness, Eumaeus's devotion) is equally central. Courage and cunning enable survival. Family bonds drive Odysseus's entire journey. Without loyalty, xenia would be meaningless — a host who welcomed you today could betray you tomorrow.
